text: If you own an index fund, an alleged Chinese honey trap just cost you money.
But that's not why Washington is worried.
To see why, start with what Nvidia sells.
Nvidia makes the chips that power much of the world's AI
They're so strategic, the U.S. limits which ones can be sold to China.
On November 8th, Nvidia's C.E.O., Jensen Huang, told staff he had been unfaithful to his wife.
According to The New York Times, U.S. authorities suspect the woman, Alice Huang, an executive at an Nvidia customer, was recruited by China's Ministry of State Security.
The alleged goal: learn about Huang, and influence his views on selling AI chips to China.
If true, that's a textbook honey trap.
China calls the spy story unsubstantiated. Nvidia's board says it has no reason to believe secrets were compromised.
Then it got worse.
The Times reported a second relationship, with an Nvidia vice president.
The Wall Street Journal reported the board was preparing to oust him.
And by CBS News' count, more than four hundred and fifty billion dollars in market value vanished.
Washington split. President Trump called Huang an honourable guy, and said he should stay.
Three House committee chairs asked him for a closed-door briefing on November 18th.
So here's why it matters.
The man at the center of America's AI chip business may have been targeted by an operation aimed at exactly that business.
That's the question for Nvidia's board. Not his marriage.
As of November 12th, there's no decision. Follow for the update.
